You know, it’s not like climbing a well-known peak like Everest or K2 is whatever. People die up there all the time, and it’s not like the mountain’s safety record is great. Plus, if you fall into a crevasse or get caught in an avalanche, no one’s really going to be there to save you. You pay your own way up there, and if something goes wrong, you’re on your own.

Sure, you can borrow gear for training, but when you’re actually choosing the big peaks, you need the latest in mountaineering technology—alpine tents, ropes, crampons, maybe even a satellite phone. And let’s be real, climate change is making these mountains more volatile every year. Ice is melting, unstable slopes are becoming the norm, and that’s not something you can plan for.

If you really are serious, maybe consider training to be a guide or a rescue climber. At least then, you’re in a position to take others and manage emergencies. Just don’t go it alone. Pursuing mountaineering as a standalone career is like putting yourself out there to be a public spectacle—everyone gets to watch you fail, but no one helps you up after you’re done. Just think about how few people you know stay in that line of work. It’s a billion-dollar industry from giving people lessons, but that’s all it is: people choosing an illusion of adventure.
